paragraphs.heading: What an alkene is
paragraphs.text: An alkene, also called an olefin, is a hydrocarbon with at least one double bond joining two carbon atoms. That double bond can sit inside the chain or right at its end, and alkenes with it at the end are called α-olefins. Chains with no ring and a single double bond follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ, where n is two or more. That is two hydrogens short of the matching alkane, which has the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. The smallest member is ethylene, C₂H₄, which IUPAC names ethene.

paragraphs.heading: Why alkenes matter
paragraphs.text: Alkenes are usually colorless and non-polar. They behave a bit like alkanes, but they react more readily. The smallest ones are gases or liquids at room temperature. Industry makes them by steam cracking and by dehydrogenation of hydrocarbons taken from petroleum and natural-gas condensate. They are turned into polymers such as polyethylene and serve as starting materials for many other industrial chemicals, and ethylene is made in larger amounts than any other organic compound.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the double bond
paragraphs.text: A carbon–carbon double bond is really two bonds of different kinds: a sigma bond and a pi bond. In one bonding model each carbon is sp² hybridized, and its three sp² orbitals make sigma bonds to three atoms, the other carbon and two hydrogens. A leftover 2p orbital on each carbon, standing at right angles to the plane of those three, joins its partner to form the pi bond, which is split with half on each side of the molecule. At 65 kcal/mol the pi bond is much weaker than the sigma bond. Together, though, the pair beats a single bond, at 611 kJ/mol against 347 kJ/mol, and is shorter, at 1.33 Å against 1.53 Å.

paragraphs.heading: A bond that will not twist
paragraphs.text: Turning one end of the double bond would pull the two p orbitals out of line, and that costs energy, so rotation around the bond is restricted. As a result, cis and trans forms change into one another so slowly that chemists can handle them at ordinary conditions without them swapping. Cis is Latin for "on this side of" and marks two groups on the same side of the double bond, while trans, "on the other side of", marks groups on opposite sides. In 2-butene, for example, the cis form has both methyl groups on one side and the trans form has them on opposite sides, and the two forms have different properties.

paragraphs.heading: The E and Z labels
paragraphs.text: When all four groups attached to the double bond are different, chemists use the more general E and Z labels instead. Each group gets a rank from the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules. If the two higher-ranked groups are on the same side, the bond is Z, from the German zusammen, "together"; if they are on opposite sides, it is E, from entgegen, "opposite". Cis and trans do not line up in any fixed way with Z and E.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and names
paragraphs.text: Around each carbon of the double bond the bonds spread at about 120°, as the VSEPR model of repelling electron pairs predicts. That angle can change, because the groups attached to those carbons crowd one another, and in propylene the C–C–C angle is 123.9°. To name a straight-chain alkene, chemists take the parent name and change its -an- to -en-. Strictly, IUPAC keeps the word alkene for chains with no ring and only one double bond, though that rule is not widely followed.
